32: NEIGHBOUR. Ah, neighbour, you must be under a spell. I've heard that Matryóna goes in for that sort of thing. It must be her.
30: ANÍSYA. Ah, but my dear, if it weren't for my heart! Him as is gone was stern enough, still I could twist him about any way I liked; but with this one I can do nothing. As soon as I see him all my anger goes. I haven't a grain of courage before him; I go about like a drowned hen.
28: NEIGHBOUR. Ah, ah, my dear, now I look at you, you are a sufferer! To suffer like that is no joke. To have given shelter to a beggar, and he to lead you such a dance! Why don't you pull in the reins?
26: NEIGHBOUR. Yes, and I've heard say he's becoming too free with his fists?
25: NEIGHBOUR. That goes without saying. ANÍSYA. Ah, how hard it is to bear such treatment from him! Oh, how it hurts!
24: ANÍSYA. So it went on from bad to worse, and I see they begin hiding from me. Ah, friend, I was that sick—that sick of my life! It's not as if I didn't love him.
23: ANÍSYA. Ah, friend, they've taken me in completely. They've done me so fine it's beyond saying. I, fool that I was, noticed nothing, suspected nothing, and so I married him. I guessed nothing, but they already understood one another. NEIGHBOUR. Oh dear, what goings on!
22: NEIGHBOUR. Eh, eh, eh, what doings! Only think of it. Why, he's her step-father!
21: ANÍSYA. Time and more than time! Ah, my dear, I'm that impatient to get her out of the house; but the matter does not come off. He does not wish it, nor she either. He's not yet had enough of his beauty, you see.
20: ANÍSYA. They made some steps too, but it didn't come off either. They won't even see us. NEIGHBOUR. Yet it's time she was married.
19: ANÍSYA [ gets up from the loom and sits down by the table ] There was some one from Dédlovo; but it seems the affair's got wind there too. They made a start, and then stopped; so the thing fell through. Of course, who'd care to? NEIGHBOUR. And the Lizounófs from Zoúevo?
18: NEIGHBOUR. Oh dear, oh dear, what a fright he did give me! I had quite forgotten. But tell me, dear, I've heard someone's been wooing Akoulína?
17: NEIGHBOUR [ starting ] Oh, how he scared me? Who is it? ANÍSYA. Why, Mítritch, our labourer.
16: MÍTRITCH [ roars ] Oh Lord! merciful Nicholas!
15: NAN. All right. I'll be back in a winking. [ Long silence ].
14: ANÍSYA. You only see if he's there.
13: NEIGHBOUR [ shakes her head ] It's a bad look-out. [ Silence ]. NAN [ at the door ] And if he's there, what am I to say?
11: ANÍSYA. Else he'd not have had any need of going. It's because of her he's unearthed all the business there. “Must go to the bank,” he says; “it's time to receive the payments,” he says. But it's all her fooling.
10: NEIGHBOUR. And he's taken Akoulína with him?
8: NAN [ jumps down from the oven and dresses ] All right.
7: ANÍSYA. You run to the inn and see! Mayhap, being drunk, he's gone there.
6: ANÍSYA. Nan! Nan, I say! NAN. Yes?
5: NEIGHBOUR. It's time he was. Hasn't he perhaps stopped at our inn? My sister, Thekla, says there's heaps of sledges standing there as have come from the town.
4: NEIGHBOUR [ enters ] Seems your goodman's not back yet? ANÍSYA. No.
2: ANÍSYA. Really, a girl's modesty reaches only to the door. Step over the threshold and it's forgotten. She is a shameless creature.
0: MÍTRITCH. What! to town? There's all sorts of things to be got in town if one's got the means. Oh Lord!
